Except you run in football and baseball. You got me on weightlifting, but Olympic weightlifting is very aerobic.

It explains the difference between the aerobic and anaerobic energy systems. Anaerobic doesn't mean no running required, it means that the energy system used is the anaerobic one. Generally any sport that uses bursts of movement lasting <2 minutes is anaerobic. Hell, sprinting itself is an anaerobic sport.

The running in baseball and football tends to be more sprinting than a jogging/endurance like activity. And sprinting is typically categorized as an anaerobic exercise (the energy expenditure exceeds the ability of the body to supply oxygen to produce that energy). This is why you can't sprint long distances (among other reasons). So I wouldn't exactly call baseball or football an aerobic sport.

As mentioned by others, better examples would have been cycling, soccer, rugby, anything with constant motion (hell, if football didn't take 5 minutes between plays it would be aerobic as well but baseball, well it's never going to fast....).

Even the initial examples provided by your friend are not clear cut. As I noted before sprinting tends to be classified as anaerobic so the 50m, 100m, 200m and maybe 400m would fall closer to anaerobic than aerobic. Similarly in swimming the 50 and 100m would likely be considered anaerobic (hell, if allowed by the rules a professional swimmer would do close to an entire length underwater without breathing because it's faster).
